metric_rationale: Tallying decides solely based on the difference in the number of feature wins ('tally_diff'). Thus, for any given subject, the true probability of choosing Option A is mathematically identical for all trial types that share the same 'tally_diff'. Any observed variance in choice proportions among trials with the same 'tally_diff' is purely due to binomial sampling noise (which for 8 repetitions is strictly bounded at 0.5 * 0.5 / 8 = 0.03125). In contrast, WADD computes a weighted sum using differing feature validities and subject-specific random weights, meaning its true preference for Option A varies substantially even among trials with the exact same 'tally_diff'. By computing the pooled within-group variance of the choice proportions (grouped by 'tally_diff'), we perfectly isolate this difference. Tallying will yield a strictly small variance (<= 0.03125), while WADD will yield a much larger variance due to the dispersion of its true underlying choice probabilities across the different trial types.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option with fewer but higher-validity features (e.g., A=[1, 1, 0, 0, 0]) over the option with more but lower-validity features (e.g., B=[0, 0, 1, 1, 1]). Tallying strictly counts the number of positive features and thus strongly prefers the option with more features, yielding a value close to 0 (modulo noise). WADD, on the other hand, weighs features by their validities. Because the validities are heavily skewed towards the first two features (0.98 + 0.85 = 1.83 vs 0.65 + 0.55 + 0.51 = 1.71), WADD will choose the fewer-but-better option much more frequently, yielding a significantly higher metric value.

The experimental design pits the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic against the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule by presenting pairs where one option excels on the highest-validity discriminating feature, while the other option excels on a larger number of lower-validity features. This metric computes the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the TTB prediction (i.e., choosing the option that is superior on the first discriminating feature). Because the trials are specifically engineered to make TTB and WADD predict opposite choices, data generated by TTB will yield a score close to 1.0 (modulo lapse rate), whereas data generated by WADD will yield a score significantly below 0.5.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) model. In this specific experimental design, every trial pits the single most valid discriminating cue against a coalition of all remaining, slightly less valid cues. TTB will consistently choose the option favored by the single best cue (yielding a metric near 1.0, modulo noise). By contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model, which integrates all cues, will find that the combined weight of the numerous opposing cues outweighs the single best cue, leading it to consistently choose the opposite option (yielding a metric near 0.0).

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the strictly deterministic Take-The-Best (TTB) prediction. Under the TTB theory, subjects will consistently choose the option favored by the single highest-validity discriminating feature (yielding a high match rate, only reduced by the lapse rate epsilon). Under Stochastic Take-The-Best (STTB), subjects probabilistically sample features based on their validities. Because the experimental design includes many trials where the highest-validity feature points to one option but multiple lower-validity features point to the other, STTB will frequently choose the non-TTB option, resulting in a significantly lower match rate.

This metric calculates the deviation rate from Take-The-Best (TTB) specifically on the most extreme conflict trials. In these trials, the highest-validity cue favors one option (the TTB choice), but almost all other cues (3 or 4) favor the opposing option. Deterministic TTB entirely ignores the sheer number of opposing cues and will only deviate due to random lapses, predicting a consistently low deviation rate. Stochastic TTB (STTB), however, samples cues probabilistically. Because there are many more cues favoring the opposing option, STTB has a high probability of sampling one of them before the single highest-validity cue, leading to a much higher deviation rate. By filtering out milder conflict trials, we maximize the expected mean gap between the theories.
